Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette:
Samir is a 52-year-old Middle Eastern American actor who has been unable to set foot in a rehearsal space since the season his wife, Layla, died. The event itself remains a jumble of sharp images and fog: he can recall with photographic clarity the fluorescent lights of the hospital corridor and the exact shade of blue on the surgeon’s scrubs, but the moments between—how he got from the waiting room to the consultation, what the doctor actually said—are missing, replaced by a sickening gap that he has never been able to fill. Layla had gone in for what should have been a routine surgery, but a cascade of errors had left her bleeding internally while the on-call team was stretched thin. Samir had been the one to notice her oxygen saturation dropping, had run to the nurses’ station, had been told to wait. By the time someone listened, it was too late. He still replays that hallway in his mind, the slow motion of it, the disbelief, and always the guilt: *I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened*.

In the months afterward, Samir found that certain things could catch him off guard and pull him back into that corridor. The sound of a child crying in a grocery store—any child, not just one he knew—would stop his breath, because it was the same pitch of Layla’s last, muffled moan before she lost consciousness. He began to avoid grocery stores altogether, shopping only at odd hours when few people were around, because even one unexpected sound could send him retreating to the car. A news segment about hospital negligence would freeze him in front of the television, his heart pounding even as his mind screamed at him to look away. Related sounds, like the beep of any medical monitor or even the squeak of rubber-soled shoes on a linoleum floor, became unbearable. Each time a trigger hit, the memories that had been fragmented would suddenly lock into place as if a photograph was being slid under his nose: the blue scrubs, the hallway, Layla’s hand going slack. Once the memory had surfaced, he couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into his body rather than gone away. And every time, the same appraisal would rise: *The people or institutions that should have protected her let me down, and the ones responsible faced no consequences*. That belief alone made him feel profoundly unsafe, even when friends or colleagues told him he was safe now—he found it impossible to believe them.

His own behaviors began to change in ways that at first seemed like common sense. He would no longer stay alone in his apartment, because being by himself meant that nothing distracted him from the replaying, so he started taking small, ignorable roles that required him to be in crowded green rooms or on busy sets. Yet crowds themselves were terrifying—he could not shake the feeling that something terrible could happen at any moment and no one would act in time—so he would keep to the edges, nodding along to whatever his fellow cast members wanted, saying yes to every suggestion because the alternative—disagreeing, standing out, risking conflict—felt too exposed. He had come to believe that if he angered anyone, they might not help him when he needed it, just as the hospital staff had not helped Layla. This people pleasing became automatic: he gave up his preferred scenes, changed his schedule at a moment’s notice, spent his evenings at restaurants he hated because saying no felt like inviting disaster. He had been avoiding any mention of the event for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh.

The more he avoided being alone, the more he ended up in triggering environments—he could not predict when a child’s cry or a sound from the street would pierce the noise of a coffee shop. Each fresh trigger reawakened the fragmented memory and reinforced his sense that no one could be trusted, which made his concentration splinter even further. On stage, he would lose his place in a monologue; in conversation, he would suddenly go quiet, flooded by negative emotions—fear, anger, shame—that had no obvious link to the present moment. The threat he felt was constant, and it made him hypervigilant: every unexpected sound became a potential trigger, looping back to keep the cycle tight. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof he had that his life had changed beyond repair, and that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe. His avoidance strategies, meant to reduce the danger, paradoxically deepened his conviction that he had failed Layla, because he would over time stop seeking any justice or even speaking her name, and that silence felt like a second betrayal. Without ever testing the feeling, he had no way to know that the threat was not what his body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off. He could not forgive himself for his inaction then, and he could not forgive himself for his inaction now.

What finally brought Samir to seek help was a missed cue during a community theater performance—a long, staring pause while the audience waited, and he had been frozen in the middle of a line because someone backstage dropped a metal tray that sounded exactly like the crash of a surgical instrument. Afterward, the director pulled him aside with concern, and Samir, unable to explain, simply nodded and said he would do better. But he knew that his strategies were no longer working; the world was getting narrower, the triggers more frequent, and his ability to smile and agree was wearing thin. He is terrified that if he does not find a way to break out of this loop, he will lose the one thing that still gives him a foothold—his work as an actor—and he will be left entirely alone, which is the one state he has been running from from the start. He hopes, more than anything, that someone can help him look at the memories without the guilt and the fear, so that he might one day walk into a rehearsal room without hearing that sound again.

violations.explanation: No paragraph shows a trigger directly causing a maladaptive strategy; strategies are driven by memory, threat, and appraisals.
No paragraph shows that the traumatic memory directly leads to a sense of threat; threat arises from appraisals tied to the memory but not the memory itself.
No paragraph shows that threat causes negative appraisals; instead, appraisals cause threat.
No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies directly trigger or exacerbate the intrusive memory; strategies lead to more triggers which then cause memory, but not direct.
No paragraph explicitly shows that maladaptive strategies increase threat; they deepen appraisals but not threat directly.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph shows a trigger directly causing a maladaptive strategy; strategies are driven by memory, threat, and appraisals.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Memory → Threat: No paragraph shows that the traumatic memory directly leads to a sense of threat; threat arises from appraisals tied to the memory but not the memory itself.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that threat causes negative appraisals; instead, appraisals cause threat.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies directly trigger or exacerbate the intrusive memory; strategies lead to more triggers which then cause memory, but not direct.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph explicitly shows that maladaptive strategies increase threat; they deepen appraisals but not threat directly.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
